**Daily Devotional**

**January 10**

*10 Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other. (Psalms 85:10 KJV)*

This verse is speaking of what Jesus did for us, as God did not want to destroy mankind, but had to deal with our sin. The only way He could do that was to send His Son Jesus to earth, to take our punishment for sin (John 3:16), so that we could become righteous through Jesus (Romans 3:22), and be able again to be in fellowship with God (John 17:3), which is eternal life.

Righteousness and peace have kissed and made up through the atonement that Jesus brought. This is a wonderful word picture of what Jesus did through His becoming our sacrificial lamb, and suffering our punishment for us. Only God could have come up with such a marvelous plan of redemption for His creation, and praise God that He did just that. When you can understand just what the sacrifice of Jesus accomplished, the doing away with the sin of the whole world, it is just mind boggling. It sure shows how much God loves us, to have gone to the expense of sending His own Son to die for us, and it makes the love of God, who is love (1 John 4:8), beyond our ability to understand with our finite minds. Thank you Father for having such love for us humans, and proving it by sending Jesus to die for us, so we could again fellowship with you.

Devotional by Pastor Joe W. Green, www.Infinite-Faith.com

The discussion at the table revolves around Matthijs van Nieuwkerk, the host, (MvN), Job Smeets (JS), Nynke Tynagel, the brunette woman (NT), and Claudia de Breij, the blonde woman (CdB).

Both JS and NT are part of Studio Job. MvN hosts this show every week. There's a different cohost every week, this week it's CdB.

MvN: Times Magazine and Financial Times acknowledged them to be one of the most influential designers in the world. By now, Studio Job has exposed its work in over 300 museums, of which New York's MoMA and London's Victoria and Albert Museum. At the moment, their work is exposed at the Groninger Museum. Sitting next to me is Studio Job: the Dutch-Belgian designer duo Job Smeets and Nynke Tynagel. Welcome.

JS: Thank you.

MvN: First a small introduction. We received some work of art from the both of you: a chair, on which we're sitting as we speak, the beautiful tit-lamp - what should it be called?

JS: Tits and beer.

MvN: Yes, tits and beer. What else could a man desire?

JS: An oath... An oath to the German Oktoberfest.

MvN: Yes, beautiful (with a somewhat ironic tone)

CdB: So the lamp and the... sculpture are part of the same thing?

JS: No, not per se.

CdB: Oh, OK. You can get them separate, as well.

JS: Yes.

CdB: But then it's either tits or beer. And now it both tits and beer.

JS: Yes, now it's tits and beer. I thought, this is nice for tonight, so I made a drawing and designed it.

MvN: Good. How did you think of the tits?

JS: Well, in the Studio Job Lounge in the Groninger Museum, we needed some lamps really fast, and with this design, it was really easy to motivate the glassblowers. And you know, this design also gives the feeling of coming home.

MvN: With these lamps attached to the wall, you mean?

JS: Yes, it's like coming home to your mother (laughs)

MvN: Do you like them, Claudia?

CdB: Ehhhh... Well I can't say. The lamps make me think of those Philippe Starck lamps, you know, the ones with the gun. At first, you think: they are so ugly! And then, you think: no, they rock! But, that's why it's called design and not just another piece of furniture. You think: I like the tits, but the gold is very ugly, but maybe it fits together. (speaking a lot really fast). To conclude, yes, I'd hang it on the wall.

MvN: Yes, I believe you would! Let's take a look at the Groninger Museum itself, with the both of you walking around inside.

JS: OK. I haven't seen it yet, so I'm excited!

(Video starts)

JS, speaking in the background: I like this kind of extremism. It's a good thing I'm not a religious person, else I'd be a fundamentalist for sure. (points at table) What you see here are dead bodies of cats. Skeletons. This is a room for a man who likes to collect our stuff. The chair itself weighs 80 kilograms. So trying to move it under the table is like, eh... you'll surely break your hips.

MvN: Yes, this collector has asked you another favour. I've been told that he lives in a beautiful mansion on the outskirts of Amsterdam, with a nice estate around it, and he asked you to design a fence for it. And you came up with a fence which has a lot to do with the German concentration camps.

JS: Ooh, I wouldn't call it like that per se.

MvN: OK, then let's take a look. This is the fence and the door, right?

JS: Yes, this is the design.

MvN: We see two chimneys, smoke, which creates the arch, we see a bell, and on it is written in Latin: suum cuique, which translates to the German...

JS: In Dutch, it means: to each his own.

MvN: Jedem das Seine, and that was - let's be honest here - on the fence of the Buchenwald concentration camp.

NT: Factually, it's a really light-hearted saying.

(everybody starts speaking at the same time, can only hear a few things:) CdB: Yes, but then Arbeit macht Frei is really light-hearted too! MvN: Yes, but with that intention...

JS: ...but you have to see it differently!

MvN: Let's go back one step. What did the collector ask you to do?

JS: The task was to provide a fence around his estate. And then, it's our duty to ask some fundamental questions about what a fence really is. And: why do we need one in our society? It's not something to be proud of. You shouldn't be proud of needing to isolate something. You can see it as protecting somebody, but you can also see it as locking someone up. And because we as a design team are always searching for icons, for instance, just look at the tits and the beer, we are also searching for a fence's icon. And you don't need to look far in our history to find concentration camps, of course! And Guantanamo Bay...

MvN: And, this collector, he is happy with this?

JS: A good collector doesn't need to be happy about something. A good collector gives the designer the freedom to do whatever he wants with it when he asks for a fence.

MvN, interrupting: But Job, then I will ask you a different question. Say that the fence will be installed in a couple of weeks. And citizens walk next to it. After all, it's placed right next to the streets. And they are offended by it, maybe even because they remember. Or maybe because they survived the camps themselves. Or at least, they recognise it.

JS: Well, well, well...

MvN: That will lead to commotion.

JS: (finding words) OK, of course, you look for the extreme when you're working. You're looking for contrasts. Contrast between good and evil. Contrast between rich and poor, between fiction and non-fiction. And if you want to give form to evil, you try to find a symbol for evil in our recent history. You'll end up here pretty quick.

CdB: (hard to translate) ... it's a designer's autonomy...

NT: You don't have to always bring good news.

CdB: Exactly. Was that what was going through your head when designing a fence?

JS: Designers are often asked to find solutions for problems. But we, we'd rather ask questions than give answers.

(everybody speaking through each other) NT: But it does make a nice design. JS: ... there are even touring cars driving to Buchenwald! Just google for it!

CdB: But that's something different! Because those people in the touring car aren't like: Yay, we're going to Disney Land! It's to see, how bad it was!

NT: But you don't watch to war movies with a bucket of popcorn right next to you? I mean....

JS: It's part of our history, it's part of who we are, and I think that we should be able to talk about it. Moreso, you shouldn't forget it!

MvN: Well, we are not condoning you, but we were very eager to find out why you came up with this...

JS: In the end, it's just the door of that guy from Once Upon a Time in the West, the guy who gets hung by his brother.

MvN: Maybe. Something different. You're often cooperating with fashion designers Viktor and Rolf. I want to show some more of what you guys do. In this show, basically everything apart from the clothing is made by you. And that is a very special thing. Let's take a look.

(video starts)

MvN: I'm following my curiosity. This tablecloth. It's right here on the table, you can't really see a lot, but the Groninger Museum didn't want to showcase it. They said that it went too far for them to expose. Am I saying that right?

JS: It went too far for them to apply it in the Studio Job Lounge, yes.

MvN: Yes, exactly. This is what it looks like. It's a bird's eye view from, again, a concentration camp.

CdB: (laughs) God almighty.

JS: Well, you don't need to create a flower tablecloth design every time.

MvN: No, definitely not.

CdB: I saw it from the sides, so I only saw the barbed wire, and thought: hey, this is nice for Christmas! But only now I see what it really is! (laughs)

JS: It's a cleaned-up-version. (referring to the tablecloth). But the discussion about it is more important. 50 meters further is the museum hall, where it is allowed: erect dicks, vaginas, concentration camps, swastikas, whatever you want. So why is it such a problem to show it in my place? It's considered 'art' in the museum, but in my lounge, it's forbidden! That's what the discussion is about!

MvN: Do you think that the Groninger Museum is petty in their decision?

JS: Well, I found the discussion to be thrilling, and in the end, they won.

CdB: But does the museum think that design should be less confronting than art?

JS: Yes...

CdB: Do you regard that as an insult to design?

JS: I don't see it as insulting but I'm finding it un-free. And I think... As a journalist, you have freedom of expression, and I think that a designer has freedom of 'form-expression' or 'sculpture-expression'.

CdB: And do you want to defuse the symbols by just using them for a table cloth, or am I thinking too far?

NT: No... it's just thematics.

JS: It's part of our iconography.

MvN: Concluding. I want to end this with a high note, even though it's an interesting discussion. Van Rompuy...
